ketzot_hachoshen.en:
If he says, "You waived it for me," he is not believed merely by ordinary possession. The same applies if he says, "You sold it to me," or, "You gave it to me as a gift." Since the party claiming the nuisance is himself also injured by the common wall arrangement and has no exclusive possession that would create a presumption, his unilateral claim does not suffice.

Similarly, before the wall is built, if one party claims, "I already paid you my half so that you should build the whole wall from your funds," he is not believed. The rule allowing a plea of payment applies after the wall has been completed and one party seeks reimbursement of money. Then the underlying building obligation has already been converted into an ordinary oral debt for expenditures, and the defendant can say he paid.

Before construction, however, the legal duty itself is to participate in building the partition. A person cannot escape that judicially imposed building obligation merely by saying, "I paid you so that you should perform my construction duty." The claim resembles one made against a standing judgment or other beit din obligation. Moreover, if such a plea were believed before construction, he would have a migo to say the other party waived the obligation entirely, which the law plainly rejects. Thus no such payment or waiver claim is available before the wall is actually built.

He explains that this differs from ordinary visual damage through a window, where the Rosh recognizes chazakah. Although the Tur holds that this injury too resembles smoke, Perishah writes that it is not quite as severe as smoke. I do not know why he omitted the Rosh at the beginning of Bava Batra, who writes that although one who tells another, "Tear my garment," can retract his permission and the other becomes liable for damage done after the retraction, the present case is different because the obligation to build a wall is a monetary claim that can be waived. Perishah himself cites this Rosh. According to the Rosh's explanation, which compares ordinary neighbor damage to the case of "tear my garment and be exempt," a mere waiver without kinyan would not be effective for other forms of damage unless they can likewise be characterized as a monetary claim subject to waiver. ketzot_hachoshen.en:
Rama says that if there is no local custom, the wall should be built as appears proper to the judges. Sema questions the source. Tur cites Rabbeinu Yonah that without a known custom the wall should be six handbreadths thick, and Ramban qualifies that if the wall is built with lime rather than mortar the required thickness can be reduced according to expert assessment. Sema therefore assumes Ramban still accepts a minimum comparable to the lightest wall described in the Mishnah.

Rama's source is Nimukei Yosef. He writes that the Mishnah's dimensions were stated in order that the wall endure. Therefore, according to authorities who understand the measurements functionally, if lime or another construction method makes a thinner wall sufficiently stable, a thinner wall may be used according to skilled builders. The judge has only what his eyes see.

Some authorities disagree and require the Mishnah's dimensions even with lime. But that dispute concerns a place where the customary materials are the Mishnah's stone types and the custom itself fixes the form. In a place with no custom at all, such as a new town, the purpose is simply to remove the visual intrusion through a wall that will endure. There is no reason to require one of the Mishnah's precise historical measurements. Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch omit the Mishnah's exact stone dimensions and instead speak generally of local custom, which supports Rama. Where there is no custom, expert judicial assessment governs from the outset.

The Maggid Mishneh explains that the Rambam's phrase "by himself" means that one partner did not tell the other, "Go take possession and acquire," and that each took possession without the other's presence. Even so, the division is effective, although such possession would not ordinarily be effective in a regular sale, as explained in siman 192. The reason is that here no transfer from one owner to another is occurring, only clarification of which portion belongs to each. According to this, when the Mechaber concludes, "some say," the added novelty is that even if both did not take possession of their respective portions, but only one took possession of his part, the other also acquires his. The Maggid Mishneh reports that some interpret the Rambam's own words "by himself" this way, reading "and this one took possession" as though it meant "or this one took possession." The Mechaber's phrase "some say that even if one took possession" does not mean that these authorities necessarily read the Rambam this way. Rather, it states their independent view that the division works even with all these deficiencies.

turei_zahav.en: (And if they customarily build a light partition). These words astonish me both regarding their source, the Ra'ah in Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of Bava Batra, and regarding Rama's formulation. The Ra'ah writes that where the custom is to build a stone wall and one neighbor says, “I will build within my own property, using brick,” the other may object, saying, “I want a wall upon which I can place supports.” Although the builder offers permission to rely upon it, the other may say, “I do not wish to accept gifts,” as in siman 171. This is astonishing. In siman 171 the case is a courtyard too small for compulsory division, namely four cubits, where one wishes to divide and give the other four cubits. The other necessarily needs to use the full four cubits and may say, “I do not wish to benefit from my fellow's gift; I will therefore refuse division and continue using it jointly.” Here, however, the only duty is to remove visual intrusion. Once one builds on his own property and removes the intrusion with a stone wall, who can object? The assertion that the other wants a wall on which to support beams is exceedingly difficult. From where did he acquire such a right? The Sages required both parties to build a partition to prevent visual intrusion, not to provide the benefit of supporting beams. Consider a case where one neighbor leaves his courtyard and does not wish to use it at all. Can the other compel him to join in building a partition? The same applies here. Once he constructs a separating wall and removes the visual intrusion, it is as though he no longer resides there. I am also astonished at Rama. The Ra'ah stated this only where the custom is a stone wall and one party seeks the customary wall so that he can support upon it. Rama, however, wrote it where the custom is to make a light partition, which is unfit for supporting anything. Why should the other prevent him from building at his own expense? This is nothing but astonishing.

ומ"מ כ"א. כמ"ש בסי' קנד סז בהג"ה אבל הוא אסור כו':
beur_hagra.en:
